entities.name: PMID:27516129
observations: In 60 participants aged 15–65 years with moderate sensorineural hearing loss, good hearing-aid performers defined by Acceptable Noise Level showed stronger speech-evoked FFR F0 encoding and greater F0/F1 spectral energy than poor performers for /da/ and /si/ at 65 dB SPL; hearing-aid output spectra were similar at the ear canal.

entities.name: PMID:29677689
observations: In 35 older adults with moderate age-related hearing loss, six months of hearing-aid use altered speech-evoked FFRs to /ga/ in quiet and babble; physiological changes correlated with behavioral changes, but participants were not preclassified as good or poor performers.

entities.name: PMID:36946195
observations: In 18 children with mainly sensorineural hearing loss, aided speech-evoked envelope-following responses improved versus unaided responses, and aided EFR improvement predicted hearing-aid-facilitated speech-discrimination improvement; no direct good-versus-poor outcome comparison was performed.

entities.name: PMID:40594752
observations: In 26 adults, speech-evoked brainstem responses to /da/ were sensitive to noise-reduction processing, and F0 amplitude ratios correlated with behavioral accuracy under noise reduction; predefined good and poor hearing-aid groups were not compared.

entities.name: Brainstem speech encoding difference
observations: The available evidence supports a likely difference in auditory-brainstem speech encoding between good and poor hearing-aid performers, primarily because one direct FFR study found stronger F0/F1 representation in good performers; the broader EFR and speech-in-noise evidence is indirect.
